metadata.title: On Some Sequences of Integers
metadata.source_note: Extracted from PDF->text fallback; .tex source not available. Math fidelity reduced.
metadata.registry_mismatch_note: metadata.json claims this paper is Behrend 1946 ('On Sets of Integers Which Contain No Three Terms'), but the PDF first page is Erdos & Turan 1936, 'On Some Sequences of Integers', J. London Math. Soc. Vol. 11 (received 6 June 1936). The two papers are closely related (both concern sets avoiding 3-term arithmetic progressions) but the source PDF is Erdos-Turan, not Behrend. Extraction reflects the PDF's actual contents.

nodes.name: A-sequence
nodes.statement: A sequence of integers $a_1 < a_2 < \dots \le N$ is called an $A$-sequence belonging to $N$ if it contains no three terms in arithmetic progression, i.e. no $a_i, a_j, a_k$ with $a_j - a_i = a_k - a_j$.
nodes.statement_clean: An A-sequence in [1,N] is an increasing integer sequence containing no three-term arithmetic progression.

nodes.name: Maximum A-sequence count $r(N)$
nodes.statement: $r(N)$ denotes the maximum number of elements in an $A$-sequence belonging to $N$ (a maximum subset of $\{1,\dots,N\}$ free of 3-term arithmetic progressions).
nodes.statement_clean: r(N) is the size of the largest 3-AP-free subset of {1,...,N}.

nodes.name: Generalized maximum count $r_l(N)$
nodes.statement: $r_l(N)$ denotes the maximum number of integers $\le N$ such that no $l$ of them form an arithmetic progression (the natural generalization of $r(N)=r_3(N)$ to longer progressions).
nodes.statement_clean: r_l(N): the largest subset of {1,...,N} with no l-term arithmetic progression.

nodes.name: van der Waerden number $f(k,l)$
nodes.statement: $f(k,l)$ is the least integer $N$ such that any partition of $\{1,\dots,N\}$ into $l$ classes forces at least one class to contain an arithmetic progression of $k$ terms.
nodes.statement_clean: Smallest N forcing a k-AP in some color class under any l-coloring of {1,...,N}.

nodes.name: Theorem I (linear upper bound)
nodes.statement: $r(2N) \le N+1$ for $N \ge 8$ (after the special checks at $N=4,5,6,7$ given in the proof).
nodes.statement_clean: For N >= 8, the maximum 3-AP-free subset of {1,...,2N} has at most N+1 elements.

nodes.name: Theorem II (improved density bound)
nodes.statement: For every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $N_0(\varepsilon)$ such that for $N > N_0(\varepsilon)$, $r(N) < (\tfrac{3}{8}+\varepsilon) N$. (Math partially reconstructed from garbled OCR; constant inferred from the worked computation showing $r(N) < \tfrac{3}{8}\cdot \text{const}$ via $r(17)=8$, $r(34)\le 16$.)
nodes.statement_clean: Asymptotically, the largest 3-AP-free subset of {1,...,N} has density at most 3/8 + epsilon.
nodes.notes: Exact constant in the OCR'd statement is illegible; reconstructed as 3/8 from the auxiliary computation r(17)=8 and the doubling argument r(34) <= 16, r(35) <= 16, r(71) <= 32, r(2^{k+2}+2^{k-1}-1) < 2^{k+1}.

nodes.name: Reflection symmetry of A-sequences
nodes.statement: If $a_1 < a_2 < \dots < a_r$ is an $A$-sequence in $\{1,\dots,N\}$, then $N+1-a_r < N+1-a_{r-1} < \dots < N+1-a_1$ is also an $A$-sequence.

nodes.name: Translation invariance
nodes.statement: For any integer $k < a_1$, $a_1 - k < a_2 - k < \dots < a_r - k$ is an $A$-sequence.

nodes.name: Subadditivity of $r$
nodes.statement: $r(m+n) \le r(m) + r(n)$ for all positive integers $m, n$.

nodes.name: Small-N values of $r$
nodes.statement_clean: Exact values of r(N) for small N, established by case analysis.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem I
nodes.statement: By induction on $N$, using the symmetry observations $(1)$ and $(2)$, the subadditivity inequality $r(m+n) \le r(m)+r(n)$, and exact small-case values $r(8)=4$, $r(14)=8$ as base cases.

nodes.name: Establish symmetry and translation reductions
nodes.statement: Observe that reversing an $A$-sequence within $\{1,\dots,N\}$ via $a_i \mapsto N+1-a_i$ gives another $A$-sequence (eqn (1)), and that translating $a_i \mapsto a_i - k$ for $k < a_1$ gives another $A$-sequence (eqn (2)). These reductions allow WLOG choices in the case analysis.

nodes.name: Derive subadditivity $r(m+n)\le r(m)+r(n)$
nodes.statement: Splitting an $A$-sequence in $\{1,\dots,m+n\}$ into its parts in $\{1,\dots,m\}$ and $\{m+1,\dots,m+n\}$ and applying translation gives $r(m+n) \le r(m)+r(n)$.

nodes.name: Base cases by case analysis: $r(8)=4$, $r(10)=5$, $r(12)=6$
nodes.statement: Direct case analysis using (1) and (2) shows $r(8)=4$ (since the candidates $1,2,4$ or $1,3,4$ both fail to extend to size 5), and similarly $r(10)=5$ and $r(12)=6$. The witnesses $1,2,4,5$ for $r(8)$ and $1,2,4,9,10$ for $r(10)$ are exhibited explicitly.

nodes.name: Establish $r(14)=8$ and $r(13)=7$
nodes.statement: The sequence $1,2,4,5,10,11,13,14$ is an $A$-sequence, giving $r(14) \ge 8$; combined with the upper bound from case analysis, $r(14)=8$ and $r(13)=7$. By (3), $r(16)\le 8$, $r(18)\le 9$, $r(20)\le 10$, $r(22)\le 11$.

nodes.name: Inductive step: $r(2N)\le N+1$
nodes.statement: Assume the theorem for $2N-8$. Then by subadditivity, $r(2N) \le r(2N-8) + r(8) \le (N-3) + 4 = N+1$, completing the induction once the base cases $N \in \{8,9,10,11\}$ (i.e. $2N \in \{16,18,20,22\}$) are verified.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem II (sketch)
nodes.statement: First show $r(17)=8$ via a refinement of the case analysis; deduce $r(34)\le 16$ and $r(35)\le 16$; iterate the doubling-with-overlap to get $r(71)\le 32$ and in general $r(2^{k+2}+2^{k-1}-1) < 2^{k+1}$. A longer but similar argument gives $r(18)=r(19)=r(20)=8$, $r(21)=9$, $r(22)=r(23)=9$, from which the density bound follows.

nodes.name: Show $r(17)=8$
nodes.statement: Since $r(14)=8$, $r(17)\ge 8$. If $r(17)=9$, then both $1$ and $17$ must occur (using $r(14)=8$); but then $9$ cannot occur (since $1,9,17$ is an AP), so by (2) $r(17)\le r(8)+r(8)=8$, contradiction.

nodes.name: Deduce $r(34)\le 16$ and $r(35)\le 16$
nodes.statement: By subadditivity $r(34)\le 2 r(17)= 16$. For $r(35)$: if $r(35)\ge 17$, then since $r(34)\le 16$ both $1$ and $35$ must lie in any maximum sequence; but then $18$ cannot occur (else $1,18,35$ is an AP), so $r(35)\le 16$.

nodes.name: Iterate to get $r(2^{k+2}+2^{k-1}-1) < 2^{k+1}$
nodes.statement: Repeating the doubling-with-forbidden-midpoint argument gives $r(71)\le 32$ and inductively $r(2^{k+2}+2^{k-1}-1) < 2^{k+1}$, which yields the density estimate $r(N) < (\tfrac{3}{8}+\varepsilon) N$ for $N$ large.
nodes.notes: Exact form of the index expression $2^{k+2}+2^{k-1}-1$ is partially garbled in the OCR; this is a best-effort reconstruction.

nodes.name: Witness $A$-sequence for $r(41)=16$
nodes.statement: The sequence $1,2,4,5,10,11,13,14,28,29,31,32,37,38,40,41$ is an $A$-sequence in $\{1,\dots,41\}$ of length $16$, showing $r(41)\ge 16$ (and thus $r(41)=16$ given the matching upper bound from $r(20)=8$).

nodes.name: Ternary-no-2 construction for $r\{(3^k+1)/2\}\ge 2^k$
nodes.statement: If $u < (3^k+1)/2$ has no digit $2$ in its ternary expansion, then the integers $u+1$ form an $A$-sequence; this gives $r\{(3^k+1)/2\} \ge 2^k$.
nodes.notes: Exponent in the bound partially reconstructed from OCR ('> P' is read as '>= 2^k').

nodes.name: Szekeres' conjecture (3-AP case)
nodes.statement: $r\{(3^k+1)/2\} = 2^k$. (Proved by Erdos-Turan for $k=1,2,3,4$.)
nodes.statement_clean: Szekeres conjectured the maximum 3-AP-free subset of {1,...,(3^k+1)/2} has exactly 2^k elements.

nodes.name: Szekeres' conjecture (general $l$-AP)
nodes.statement: More generally, for any prime $p$ and $l \ge 3$, $r_l\{(p^k - 1)/(p-1)\cdot \text{[expr]}\} = (p-1)^k$. (Math partially reconstructed: the index expression on the LHS is garbled in the OCR; the RHS $(p-1)^k$ is clear.)
nodes.notes: The formula '$r_l\{(p^k-2p^{k-1}+\dots)/(p-1)\}=(p-1)^k$' is illegible in the OCR; only the RHS $(p-1)^k$ and the prime/$p$-adic structure of the LHS are recoverable.

nodes.name: Density conjecture $r(N)=o(N)$
nodes.statement: It is probable that $r(N) = o(N)$, i.e. the maximum size of a 3-AP-free subset of $\{1,\dots,N\}$ is sublinear in $N$.
nodes.statement_clean: Open question: does r(N)/N tend to zero as N grows?
nodes.notes: This conjecture was later settled affirmatively by Roth (1953); from the perspective of this 1936 paper it is open.

nodes.name: Consequence: infinitely many $k$-AP's of primes
nodes.statement: If Szekeres' general conjecture holds, then for every $k$ there are infinitely many $k$-term arithmetic progressions of primes.

nodes.name: Consequence: improved van der Waerden bound
nodes.statement: Szekeres' general conjecture would yield a new proof of van der Waerden's theorem with the sharper bound $f(k,l) \le l^{e^{k \log k}}$ (exact form of the exponent partially reconstructed from garbled OCR; the original prints 'leeklog E' which we read as $l^{e^{k \log k}}$).
nodes.notes: OCR garbled the exponent; reconstruction $l^{e^{k\log k}}$ is best-effort.

nodes.name: van der Waerden's theorem (cited)
nodes.statement: For all $k, l \ge 1$, the function $f(k,l)$ exists, i.e. there is an $N$ such that any $l$-coloring of $\{1,\dots,N\}$ contains a monochromatic $k$-AP.
